data.name: Diary of a Garden Nerd: Planning a Desert Flower & Foodscaped Front Garden for Fall
data.about: We're transforming a bleak front yard into a beautiful and productive desert foodscape for Fall 2025, blending flowers and edibles into a sustainable garden design.
tools: Google Sheets (or a similar spreadsheet app)

paragraphs.text: Step 1 - Visualize your Dream Garden:

Carrie, Arthur's ex-wife and I have been cultivating a positive relationship over the last few years while we coordinated on cultivating a culinary garden in the back yard of Arthur's house in Chandler AZ (where she rents a room). We've had some epically fruitful harvests from the back garden, so when Carrie texted me suggesting we work together to transform the scraggly front yard of Arthur's house into a desert flower garden and foodscape, I was immediately excited, started making a shared Google Sheet (spreadsheet) to plan our new gardening adventure.
Step 2 - Unleash Your Inner Garden-Nerd:

I created a makeshift Kanban board (on Sheets) for tasks, and Carrie and I worked together to make a spreadsheet with a list of plants we both wanted to include (with details provided by an AI (I used Google Gemini) about when to plant, harvest, cost etc) and then I chatted with an AI about what materials we would need and I put together a materials spreadsheet as well.

I love a good spreadsheet, but plotting a garden diagram made me absolutely giddy. It allowed me to really visualize the space and try out different layouts of plants and pavers and things until I could see a vivid mental picture a beautiful, productive desert food garden. Gemini suggested a few free garden planning websites to design a virtual layout for our foodscape. The one we found easiest to use and share was Gardena's My-Garden Planner.
Step 3 - Brass Taxes: Sourcing and Budgeting

To maximize the success for each plant we plan to put in the ground, I started a 'thread' with Google Gemini about our food-landscape project (so I could build an easily searchable knowledge base). After giving Gemini a list of plants we wanted to grow, I had Gemmi generate a spreadsheet listing planting and harvesting information including whether each plant should be started from seed or cutting, how to prepare for planting: which seeds to pre-soak before planting, how long to dry succulents to form a callus before planting, which herbs to start from cuttings and whether to start indoors or sew directly outside and when.

We're going to start planting after the summer heat has died down (in mid-late October), so in the last couple weeks, I've been saving seeds from herbs and vegetables in my home garden and setting up a grow space at my house to start those seeds indoors. I've also been gleefully poking around my succulent pots and pulling up succulent 'pups' to start forming a 'cuticle on them' and in anticipation of adding them to our Desert Foodscape.

Carrie has a bead on a free 'chip drop' of wood chips to put over her dying lawn. The wood chips will be our base layer, which will help suppress weeds and retain moisture. We're going to request our chip drop for late August or early September so the chips can begin to settle and decompose before planting.

We will have to buy some materials from Amazon or Home Depot or wherever  (like drip line, pavers and trees), but the overall cost for the front foodscape should hopefully be within a couple hundred dollars
Step 4 - Doing What we Kanban to Stay on Track

We have a shared vision and a path forward. The next step is to actually move some earth, lay some drip line and pavers, plants some plants and transform this wasteland of a front yard into a beautiful garden.

data.name: Diary of a Garden Nerd: Starting Plants for our Fall Desert Foodscape
data.about: It's a race against the Arizona sun! Learn how we get a head start on our fall foodscape by starting plants indoors to beat the heat.
tools: trays to start plant boxes on
materials: seeds (artichoke, marigold, beets, barley, misc vegetables)
pre-mixed potting soil OR compost, sand, perlite, coco coir to make soil
3-5 gallon nursery pots (or buckets with drain holes)

paragraphs.text: The Right Place at the Right Time with the Right Light

The Arizona desert gives a tight window for fall planting. The temperatures don't usually drop below 100F until mid-October, but by January there's winter frost to worry about. To extend the season long enough to ensure a hearty harvest and protect seeds and sprouts from the gang of sparrows in our yard, I started most of our plants indoors in early August.

We are fortunate enough to have an 'Arizona Room' (a thinly enclosed patio) that I was able to insulate. Even more fortunately, Arthur's previous job was designing LED agro lights, so we happen to have a large commercial-grade grow light in our makeshift grow room.
Getting the Propagation Party Started: Sourcing Plants and Tucking Them in For a Dirt Nap:

Following Google Gemini's advice (an AI), I mixed up some homemade garden soils (a blend of compost, sand, perlite, and —for some plants— coco coir). I filled some old cut-in-half LaCroix boxes and 3-gallon nursery pots with my soil and seeded them with 20 pre-soaked artichoke seeds, a half dozen basil and mint cuttings from our yard (dipped in rooting compound and soaked in water for a couple weeks), a variety of saved and store-bought vegetable seeds and some marigolds for a pest-controlling pop of color.

The plan is to plant our perennial herbs and flowers (started in LaCroix boxes) in beds with a weed border, while succulents will be planted into beds topped with river rock (that were not being used well in our backyard). I'm going to keep the seasonal vegetables and herbs in the 3-gallon nursery pots where I started them --including peas and beans which are climbing up the homemade twig and twine vine trellis I created for them. When it's time to plant, we'll bury the pot up to its neck and cover it with wood chips.
To Pretty-up the landscape a bit (and because we live in the desert), I also pulled a variety of cactus and succulent pups from our backyard and a few from my dad's place.

There are a few herbs that I've always struggled to grow from seed, so I broke down and bought oregano, rosemary, and lemongrass from Home Depot. Fortunately, the oregano and lemongrass I purchased had multiple plants in each pot, so I was able to triple up our starting supply by replanting each into its own 3-gallon nursery pot!
Training for Transplanting

I've begun taking the indoor 'starts' --that are big enough to be less appealing to sparrows and other pests-- on field trips outdoors. As we get closer to planting time I'll increase the number of hours each day. This process, called 'hardening off,' helps nursery plants adjust to the sun and wind before they go to their forever home.
By October, when the sun has stopped trying to kill us all and the yard is prepped, our plant babies should be ready to grow and thrive!

data.name: Diary of a Garden Nerd: Wood Chips and Shovel Dips

paragraphs.text: A Mountain of Wood Fit For the King of Beavers

We put the labor in labor day weekend last week 🥵 Thanks to a Haboob (windstorm) that ripped branches off trees all around our area last week, our 'free chip drop' (wood chips from a local tree trimming company's haul that day) we got a mountain of chewed up Palo Verde limbs that were just about as much as this woodchuck could chuck.
I woke up with a delightful twitter in my tummy. For a garden nerd like me, it was like Christmas morning --I finally got to start playing with the toys I'd been dreaming about.
It was finally time to get dirty.
Sweat, Muscle, and a Reality Check

As I dug the teeth of my rake into the smelly steaming chip pile and watched a heavy swipe of wood chips cascade down the pile. I was sure I'd single-handedly have the whole job knocked out by noon, but my eyes were bigger than my shovel. After a solid 2 ½ hours on the first day, my canteen was out of water and my muscles were out of gas, but there was still plenty of chipped wood to work on, though.

The next day my whole body ached --which means I got a good full workout (which is not not something I'm after). Just two more sessions of raking and spreading (and filling and hauling construction bags full of chips to the farthest reaches) and we had the entire patchy lawn covered with 6-8 inches of wood chips... and now we wait.
The Lawn has a Plan of its Own

The plants are on track in our indoor nursery and we have to wait for the wood chips to break down and settle into place before we can set paver stones and start bringing the plants into the landscape when temperatures cool down in early - mid October.

The one hitch in our operation (so far...in step one) is: though I had read that wood chips will kill a lawn, I didn’t pay attention to the details. It can take months for the chips to slowly block out the light and smother a lawn --and since we're working during monsoon season, the damp, nutrient-rich chip pile already had grass climbing up its side the day after it arrived. I'm going to put that hitch in my giddyup though and finally build the DIY chicken tractor I've been thinking about for years. Then I can have Broodzilla and her brood (and/or some of our other hens) help me pull weeds.

data.name: Garden Glamping for Hens: DIY Collapsable Chicken Tractor
data.about: The flock that weeds together succeeds together
materials: 3 or 4x 1/2 inch boards (cut to fit tent)

paragraphs.text: Getting In-Tent
Lows are in the high 70s and the wood chips base for our desert foodscape continues to sprout grass, so I've decided to get our hens to do some weeding for us.

To form a shade canopy and the exterior frame of this 'chicken tractor', I used a 20 year old 2-person Ikea tent (which had gotten pretty grubby when I'd used it as a brooder when our hens were just baby chicks a few years back).
After assembling the tent, I used heavy scissors to cut the bottom out.
Frame Job
After measuring the interior of the tent, I used an electric miter saw to cut my 1/2-inch boards to fit.
Note - If you are buying 8x4x1/2 inch boards, and your tent is 4 ft wide or less, you will only need 3 boards otherwise you will need 4.
Assemble Interior Frame
To keep the 'chicken tractor' portable, I decided to use corner clamps to hold together the frame (so that the frame can be easily transported in my car).
Clip Clip Hooray!
Using binder clips, (two on each side) I clipped the outside of the tent to the wood frame.

With the wood frame clipped in place, my lil 'chicken tractor' is heavy and rigid enough to stop chickens from climbing under, but not so heavy that I can't stick my arm in the door and walk it along (an inch or so above the ground) to relocate it to the next weedy spot.
The Flock That Weeds Together Succeeds Together!
I have a collapsable dog crate to transport 2-3 of our hens in the car and get them into to the 'chicken tractor'.

Once I set the tent in place and put in a tray of cool water, I toss out some treats (to make sure my hens are excited about being in the tractor) and off they go to snack away on weeds inside their shaded chicken tractor.

data.name: Diary of a Garden Nerd: Coming in for a Bumpy Planting
data.about: The final stage of the desert foodscape: A hard-won victory over root rot, fungus gnats, rats, and mold, culminating in the triumphant transplanting of all the survivor plants.

paragraphs.text: The Nursery Nightmare 😱

The decorative vegetables and legumes I’d started indoors were lush and green as we approached the final planting window, so I started to harden them off (carry trays and pots of young plantlings outside to get them used to the climate and wind). Everything was going great, until I overwatered the seedlings. I’d thought the excess water would evaporate immediately when I took them outside, but it didn’t, leading to what looked like root rot—a nail in the coffin for most young plants. To make matters worse, the wet soil brought "black flies" (likely fungus gnats) into the house and introduced them to every plant I owned 🤦‍♀️

It was devastating. My beautiful, two-month-old artichoke seedlings, which I had been meticulously protecting from predators like birds, were now losing a battle with fungus. To save what plants I could (and drive the flies out of our house), I had to shut down the indoor nursery and move everything outside full time.

The late afternoon temperatures were still hitting triple digits, so it was a serious shock to my poor plant babies’ systems. About half of the plants managed to survive —until a **starving rat** cruised through one night and ate my marigolds down to the roots, decapitated several of my promising sunflowers, and snacked on half my young artichokes. It was a pretty disappointing few days, but I shoved some new seeds in the pots and hoped for the best.
The Moldy Mulch & The Mask Strategy 😷

Meanwhile at the garden site, the wood chips were decomposing and holding onto the moisture from summer monsoon storms. The grass we’d hoped to bury and suffocate with the wood chips was rapidly climbing up from the edges of the yard, over our beautiful (exhaustively raked) pile of wood chips. Meanwhile, below the chip pile, **the fungus among us was thriving.**

The combination of the thick layer of wood chips and the humidity of monsoon season created a perfect environment for fungal growth. Go-getter that I am, as soon as I saw the grass, I grabbed my weed wacker and **went after it.** Unfortunately, I kicked up a lot of dust, debris, and obviously fungus spores in the process, and I ended up with a cough and a fever — **twice before my dumb ass bought a 12-pack of N-95 masks and started wearing them on site.**  Despite the setbacks, enough plants (and I) made it to planting day to fulfill the vision I’d had for the garden!
**PSA - I was dumb. Don’t be like me!** If you're tackling a large mulching project, especially in a damp climate, **WEAR A MASK OR RESPIRATOR!**
The Great Transplant 🪴

By the first week of October, all the high temperatures in the ten-day forecast were below 100°F, but frost would be possible by January, so it was go time! In spite of the rot, the pests, and the mold— my plants made it to their forever home.

There is still some minor cleanup. I need to add a couple of splitters to the drip line to reach every last plant and then bury the tubing under the wood chips, and the plants have to survive the heat of the decomposing wood chips. But for now, the tough, little survivors of my "Nursery Nightmare" are in the ground (and I am not). For now, I’m enjoying optimistic visions of a thriving desert foodscape. The light at the end of the tunnel looks exactly like the vision I've been dreaming of for months.

data.name: From Free Salad Bar to Trashy Plant Sanctuary: How a Wire Trash Can Saved My Seedlings
data.about: After years of losing young plants to everything from rats and squirrels to sparrows, I finally found the simplest, cheapest, and most durable solution: using upside-down wire trash cans as protective domes.

paragraphs.text: Try Trying Again:

I normally love cute little creatures, but with them tearing up my garden, I’ve been starting to relate a lot more to farmer McGregor from Peter Rabbit than I’d like. Fortunately, I think my angry farmer days are done. Here’s a look back at the methods I’ve tried to protect my plants.
The Nursery Nightmare [FAIL]

Starting plants indoors seemed like the most logical approach: grow them to a resilient size before exposure. This method **works okay for some plants**, but trying to maintain a perfect nursery environment in our poorly insulated "Arizona Room" (which is more of a glorified sun porch) was a constant battle. It was hard to maintain the ideal balance of moisture and heat. Some plants drowned, others withered and bugs still got to the plants. Overall, between the setup and the cost of running supplemental grow lights, I’d say it’s **not really worth it**.
Landscape Netting and Row Covers: Gruesome and Gaping [FAIL]

Landscape netting seemed like a great, low-cost solution. I put up lightweight netting around my young beets and cabbage (whose sprouts are a delicacy among sparrows around here). The net definitely seemed to keep sparrows and other hungry birds away (a couple sparrows actually got tangled in it and died) which was way more gruesome of a solution than I was looking for. To make it worse, my brutal victory over the birds was short-lived. As my sprouts started to develop, hungry rodents, primarily rats and squirrels, chewed through the thin plastic mesh quite easily and had a micro greens feast, so I think I’m going to try to stay off the net for now.
DIY Plant Cages [Effective but Time-Consuming and Painful]

My next big effort involved galvanized hardware cloth (a sturdy half inch wire mesh that can be bought from a hardware store) which I used to fabricate custom cages. I cut and bent the mesh into rectangles of various sizes (stitching the sides and tops together with some of the wire that had been used to bind the hardware cloth.

This worked **pretty well**! Nothing chewed through that solid wire nor was any creature hurt by it. The main downside was making the cages was incredibly **time-consuming** cutting and bending the sharp wire for dozens of cages was tedious and required **tin snips, gloves and patience** (and my gloves weren’t thick enough, so I still ended up with punctures and cuts all over my hands). A roll of 2 ft. x 25 ft. 19-Gauge Hardware Cloth was about **$55.00 after taxes** made about a dozen cages.
One person's trash can is another person’s treasure chest [Winner]
Shortly after I built my DIY plant cages, a friend stumbled across a brilliant, simple idea on social media: **using upside down wire trash cans as protective plant domes.**
Why the Wire Can Triumphs:
1. **Instant Protection:** They come pre-formed as a durable, heavy-gauge wire cage. No cutting, no bending, no bloody knuckles.

2. **Affordable & Reusable:** You can often find these trash cans (the kind with wide, sturdy mesh) for less than the hardware cloth alone would cost and they last for years. I bought a **10-pack of wire trash cans for $33.00 on Amazon**.
3. **Perfect Size:** The standard small to medium cans are tall enough to allow **sunflowers and squash plants** to safely grow from tiny tasty sprouts to hearty young plants.
4. **Critter-Proof:** The wire is thick and sturdy enough that squirrels and rats can’t chew through it, and the cans are heavy enough that birds can’t easily knock them over.

Flipping wire cans upside down over young plants provides instant protection from everything from roving rats to persistent sparrows without blocking sunlight or hindering water and air flow and they can be used year after year. I don’t want to count my crop before harvest, but it looks like we may finally be getting back to **dropping some phat beets** on Arillian Farm.

data.name: From Smack Down to Blinged Out: Encapsulating a Scorpion in Epoxy Resin
data.about: This is What Happens to Scorpions Who Pick a Fight With My Feet—a quick and dirty DIY guide to turning a painful memory into a tacky trophy necklace using fast-setting epoxy.
safety_notes: Ensure the scorpion is deceased and inert before handling.
Wear gloves when handling epoxy resin.
Work in a well-ventilated area.
materials: 2-part quick-setting epoxy resin mix (Gorilla Glue style)
Small metal bracket or jewelry bail

paragraphs.text: Inspiration Strikes! 🦶 🦂

As I was walking through my living room this morning wondering what I should write my DIY article about, I felt a jolt of excitement—A scorpion had stung my toe! So obviously I decided to encapsulate it in epoxy in some artistic way and use that as my DIY topic.
Safety Notes:
Ensure the scorpion is deceased and inert before handling, Wear gloves when handling epoxy resin, Work in a well-ventilated area.
Getting Graphic

I thought it would be funny/apt to name my little scorpion art piece 'That moment when you get stung by a scorpion for the first time' and then have Gemini (Google's AI) create a cartoon image of a horrified woman to alongside the scorpion 'cause I screamed my head off when I felt a hot jolt of pain in my foot, then caught sight of the scorpion under my foot.
Squeeze the Fun Out of It

Mixing up the Gorilla Glue epoxy was fast and easy, it comes in a two-chamber syringe, so you just apply even pressure and squeeze it out into a mixing vessel then stir for 20 seconds. The little kit even comes with a stirring stick and the epoxy can stirred together in the plastic part of its packaging --PRO TIP - Wear a mask and/ or work in a well ventilated area!
The Challenge of Quick-Set Epoxy & Layout Mistakes

I don't have any other epoxy projects on the horizon, so I decided to just use a small quick-drying epoxy kit from a hardware store instead of the crafting epoxy I normally use. If I had it to do over again, I'd spring for the crafting stuff. The Gorilla Glue version that I bought was hard to get bubbles out of and wasn't really intended to be poured as thick as I needed to fill my mold, but it was quick and easy.

Truth be told, I also messed up my layout. I should have put some epoxy down, then the scorpion, then more epoxy, then the best side of my 2-sided cartoon print and then more epoxy, so that the scorpion was featured on the smooth bottom of the mold. But what I did was put epoxy down, then the bad side of the print, then the scorpion. Unfortunately, the scorpion side is uneven and the scorpion's body is slightly exposed in a couple places - meh 😑
Final Assembly: The Medal of Honor

The necklace was set enough to handle and remove from the mold within half an hour, but was still somewhat supple. I couldn't find my necklace eyelits to screw into it, but I had a small metal bracket that I was able to install with a small hammer... and now I have a big tacky scorpion necklace to wear like a medal of honor—for my bravery and triumph over this poor tiny arachnid.

paragraphs.text: Ordering First and Asking Questions Later - A Lesson in Poor Floor Planning 🤦

I've had some extra time between tenants in my rental house (because a tree fell through the roof during a 'microburst' last month and my roofer has been arguing with my insurance about whether or not to replace all the 100-year-old planks in the roof with plywood or just 'patch the shattered planks where necessary'). The lack of progress on the roof and water-damaged bedroom (where the tree branch fell through the roof) has left me feeling more and more helpless and stressed as we approach the December 1st move in date for my new tenants (friends of mine). So I decided to take advantage of the down time and ditch the dingy old carpet and lay down tile. Of course, in classic Jillian style, I was so excited about the decision that I immediately ordered 45 boxes of porcelain tile --Before I got to the dirty work of ripping up the carpet and tack strips. What I found underneath was some mostly lovely hardwood floors --that were being consumed by termites.
A Bug In The Operation - Termite Troubles

At the moment I saw the termite droppings, my reaction was something like 'F M L', but after a few deep breaths I realized that they'd been munching away under the carpet for who knows how long --and if I hadn't decided to update the flooring, the situation could have been much worse. I immediately paused my work (I read doing construction around termites can drive them deeper into your house) and called a pest control company to treat the area and put traps around my property (something I normally might have handled myself, but with my tenant move in looming, I had to just throw money at it).
The Backer Board Bombshell - You Can't Lay Ceramic Tile Directly Over Hardwood Floors

The second unexpected hitch in my tile plan came when I was talking to Arthur about my grand flooring update and he was like 'I don't think you can just put tile over hardwood because the boards expand and contract'. I told him he was wrong. The thinset (which I'd already bought) said it adheres well to wood, concrete and most surfaces but when I Googled it, the search engine actually sided with Arthur -- thus a new construction material entered my life **cement backer board**, or Hardie Board.
Suddenly my simple floor update had become a major renovation. It was going to be a tight timeline to install 800 sq feet of tile now I basically had to do twice the work.
A Giant Game of Tetris - Planning our Cement Board Layout

Arthur and I spent two days just cutting and laying out a couple dozen sheets of the heavy, awkard cement board, cutting out notches for doorways and cutting a square for the crawlspace access in the living room before I could even begin spreading thinset and adhering each board (one at a time) to the wood floor.
PRO TIP - Arthur was able to hold a shop vac hose over our Matrix Drill Circular Saw while he cut. We wore masks also, but the vacuum really helped to keep nasty dust out of the yard.
Mixing Thinset - A Dark Art

Not only is powdered thinset carcinogenic when inhaled, the wet form is also horrible for skin and hard on tools. Don't try to mix an entire 50 lb bag of thinset at once. It never turns out right. Always add water to the bucket first but start with 2 quarts and then scoop in more and more thinset, mixing each scoop as you go until its the consistency of smooth, thick peanutbutter- The first time I laid floor tile (about ten years ago at Arthur's house) we found we needed a corded drill to mix the thinset because our battery operated drill didn't have enough power. Half way through the job we still burned out the drill because the thinset is so heavy and hard to stir. Since then I've been mixing it by hand in smaller batches, but getting thinset on your arms and hands is horribly painful. It's caustic and abrasive and it bonds to your skin and eats away at it, so definitely try to avoid any direct exposure to the thinset.
A Hardie Hard Workout and a Chemical Peel All At Once - The Joys of Working with Cement Board

Arthur was only able to help me on the weekend, so I was on my own (wearing a short sleeved shirt like a dumbass who doesn't care about her arm skin) when it came time to mix up the thinset and secure the Hardie Board to the floor.  My back and arms ache from pick up the boards to cut, place and secure them and my poor exposed arms ended up with painful chemical burns, but I got about 800 sq ft of Hardie board set and screwed down in about twenty hours, over the course of 2 1/2 days --adding almost an entire work week to the floor project., but I'm finally ready to start tiling. 😩
Flooring It - Procedure for Installing Concrete Backer Board over Hardwood

1 - Layout cement board, cutting perimeter pieces precisely with a circular saw with a diamond tipped or carbide tipped blade (designed to cut fiber cement)so there's a 1/8 inch gap between Hardie boards and a 1/4 inch gap between the wall and the Hardie boards.
SAFETY NOTE - You must where a respirator mask N95 or better. Cutting cement board generates a lot of carcinogenic silica dust.

2 - Adhere cement boards to floor with thinset - Using a polymer-modified thinset and a 1/4 inch notched trowel, use the flat edges of the trowel to spread enough thinset to lay one cement board (or partial cement board) at a time. Then drag the notched side of the trowel through the smooth thinset at a 45degree angle in one direction, perpendicular to the layout of the wood floor boards and then set the hardie board in place on top of the thinset --adjusting it so that edges are spaced appropriately.

3 - Every 8 inches or so across the Hardie board, while the thinset is still wet, drive cement board screws into each cement board so the head of the screw is just below the surface of the cement board. SAFETY NOTE - YOU SHOULD WEAR A MASK IN CASE THE DRILL KICKS UP DUST
4 - When all the Hardie boards are set and screwed in place, use cement board tape to tape each seam between boards and then spread thinset over the tape and into the gaps between cement boards.

data.name: Crafting with Trash: Toilet Roll 12 Days of Christmas Advent Calendar
data.about: Turn Your Trash Into a Holiday Treasure Trove
safety_notes: Ensure all contents placed inside the tubes are age-appropriate and non-toxic, especially for small children.
Use a low-temperature glue gun if children are helping with the assembly.
tools: Hot glue gun and glue sticks
a marker to number the days
materials: One piece of sturdy cardboard (e.g., from a soda or cereal box)
Green wrapping paper or construction paper (for the tree)
Dark colored wrapping paper or construction paper (for the trunk)
Assorted small treats (candy, stickers, mini puzzles etc)

paragraphs.text: Gathering the Goods: Prepping and Sealing the Toilet Rolls

I decided to make a 12-days of Christmas Advent Calendar because I lost a month of my life to tiling the floor of my rental house, so I'm running behind on Christmas crafting and I missed the boat on making a 24 or 25 day advent calendar. The last 12 days are where things get exciting anyway.

The tubes from toilet paper rolls seem the perfect size to hide holiday trinkets (and I happen to save all my toilet tubes for crafting), so I decided to arrange them in a tree shape and glue them to a cardboard base (to either set on a table or hang on the wall).  My original thought was to use wrapping paper to cover the cardboard tubes, but I realized I don't have any Christmas paper, so I found some colored construction paper to use instead.
From Toilet Tube to Treasure Tree:: Building the Tree Structure

Once I had my materials, I arranged the 12 tubes on the cardboard (cut up soda box) in a Christmas tree shape, cutting four small slits around one end of the tube and then folding the flaps inwards like you’d seal a cereal box and then using a couple dots of hot glue to secure the sealed end of the tube to the cardboard (pro tip - I pushed and held the tubes down on the cardboard with my scissors to promote a good bond).
Adding the Magic: Filling and Covering the Calendar

Now for the fun part: filling! I used a mix of candy, stickers, and little metal brain teaser puzzles. Once filled, you need to seal the top opening. I would have used green wrapping paper if I had any, but  instead I used construction paper, cutting small squares of green and black paper (Green for the tree and blac for the trunk --because I didn't have brown paper), I taped the squares over the open end of the tubes. (So each days gift will be revealed when the paper is punched or pulled off).
Phase 4: The Ugly (But Potential Great!) Tree Calendar

My first attempt (the 'ugly tree') looks like it was made by four two year olds and not one forty two year old, but who doesn't love a good rough-around-the-edges craft at Christmas. For the next revision, I plan to use wrapping paper or paint the tubes for a smoother look, but the structure is 100% sound. The final step is to number the 'doors' from 1 to 12. Believe in the process—this easy, (ugly) upcycled craft will bring you joy for the 12 days of christmas!

data.name: Diary of a Garden Nerd: Grass Roots Are Hard to Kill
data.about: The Challenge of Growing What you Want and Not What you Don't
materials: 1 Gallon White Vinegar (the more concentrated the better)

paragraphs.text: Grass Roots Run Deep

It's been about three months the wood chip delivery for the foodscape I built with my friend and I had thought the lawn would give up and die off if I kept wacking the grass as it showed up and as the daylight hours and temp dropped. Unfortunately we've had unseasonably warm temperatures this fall and a few unusually proflic storms, so the lawn has been raging on.
Reacting with Chemicals: Making a DIY Weed Killer Using Vinegar, Salt and Dishsoap

Originally I wanted the garden to be fully organic with no use of any chemical whatsoever, but I found a recipe online to make a simple DIY weedkiller and I decided it was time to bust out the old pump sprayer:

DIY WEED KILLER: In a pump sprayer, mix 1 gallon vinegar, 1 cup salt, 1 tablespoon dish soap and spray on undesired grass and weeds NOTE - THIS SPRAY WILL KILL ANY PLANT YOU SPRAY IT ON AND MAY BUILD UP IN THE SOIL TO MAKE FUTURE GROWTH HARDER
The Mounting Resistance: Repeatedly Spraying to Lower Soil Fertility  😬 🤞

I've been consistently spraying the edge of the wood chips and patches where grass has been cropping up every other week for the last two months in hopes that the soil will become too brackish and acidic to support new growth. The grass has slowed its roll lately, but its hard to tell if the shorter daylight hours and drier weather caused the reduced growth or if my DIY spray is actually working. Time will tell I guess.
The Spoils of Labor: Enjoying the beauty and Bounty of our Garden
The good news is the garden plants have been thriving with volunteer pumpkins and tomatoes absolutely loving the fresh soil from the decomposing wood chips every bit as much as the grass.

data.name: Rescue Protocol: What to Do When You Find a Fallen Baby Bird
data.about: A technical guide on identifying, warming, and reuniting fallen squabs with their parents.
safety_notes: NEVER feed a bird that is cold to the touch; it cannot digest food and may develop 'sour crop.'
DO NOT drop water into a baby pigeon's beak as they drink by suction and can easily aspirate.
Always check for a heat source safety; ensure the bird can move away from a heating pad to avoid overheating.
tools: Plastic syringe (no needle) and rubber glove (for emergency feeding only)
materials: Small basket or berry carton (for replacement nests)
Kaytee Exact Baby Bird Food (emergency backup only)

paragraphs.text: Step 1: Identify and Assess

First, determine the age and species. A baby pigeon (squab) looks like a prehistoric creature with yellow fuzz and a large beak. If the bird is 'gaping' (opening its mouth), it is likely begging for food or stressed. If it was out all night, it will be cold and weak. Check the immediate area for a nest or parents before moving it.
Step 2: The Critical Warming Period

If you cannot immediately return the bird to its nest, warmth is more important than food. Place the bird in a box with a heating pad set to LOW under only half of the container. This allows the bird to self-regulate its temperature. A cold bird cannot digest food; you must wait 30-60 minutes until the bird feels warm (like a warm potato) before proceeding with food or a reunion.
Step 3: Reunion or Replacement Nest

The 'human scent' myth is false—parents will take a baby back! Locate the nest in rafters or eaves and place the warm bird back inside. If the nest is unreachable, secure a small basket (a replacement nest) as close to the original spot as possible. Watch from a distance for 2 hours to see if the parents return to brood or feed.
Step 4: Emergency Contacts
If the parents do not return or the bird is injured, the next best thing to do is lookup a local wildlife rehabilitator and bring the bird there.
Last Resort: Emergency Feeding

If you cannot quickly get the bird to a rehab, you can feed the bird with 'Kaytee Exact Baby Bird Food'. Pigeons feed differently than songbirds; they stick their beaks into the parent's throat to suckle. To mimic this, fill a 10ml needle-less syringe with warm formula. Stretch a piece of a rubber glove over the nozzle end and secure it with a rubber band. Cut a small slit or hole in the glove. Gently guide the squab’s beak into the hole. Once it feels the warm formula, it will begin to 'pump' its head and suck the food out of the syringe. Stop immediately if the bird pulls away or if you see fluid coming out of its nostrils to prevent drowning (aspiration).

data.name: Them's The Brakes Kid: A Quick Tutorial About How to Change Brake Pads
data.about: A step-by-step guide to changing front brake pads on a car featuring a hands-on tutorial for beginners (on a 2002 Suzuki XL7) .
safety_notes: Always set the parking brake and block the tires before lifting the vehicle.
Never work under a car supported only by a hydraulic jack; always use jack stands.
Ensure bolts are torqued to your specific vehicle's manufacturer specifications.
materials: New brake pads (matching your vehicle make/model)

paragraphs.text: Preparation and Lifting

Begin by setting the parking brake and blocking (or chocking) the tires to prevent the car from rolling. Position your hydraulic jack under the designated 'jack point' and raise the vehicle until the wheel is just barely off the ground. Loosen the lug nuts with a breaker bar or impact wrench before jacking the car high enough to fully remove the wheel. Secure the vehicle with jack stands for safety.
SAFETY TIP - DO NOT PUT ANY PART OF YOUR BODY UNDER THE CAR WHILE WORKING ON THE BRAKES
Removing the Old Pads

Locate and loosen the two bolts on the back of the wheel hub that hold the caliper in place. Carefully set the caliper aside (do not let it hang by the brake line). Slide the old brake pads out of their clips.
Installing New Pads

Not all brake pads are identical so compare your old pads with the new ones to ensure a proper match, then slide the new pads into the clips. (replace any spring clips that may have popped out or come loose) Use a C-clamp to slowly compress the caliper piston back to its seated position so it fits over the new, thicker pads. Reattach the caliper and torque the bolts back to spec. Finally, replace the wheel and tighten the lug nuts in a star pattern.
Replacing Caliper

Use a C-clamp to slowly compress the caliper piston back to its seated position so it fits over the new, thicker pads. (Turn wrench about quater turns pausing in between turns to check for wetness) Reattach the caliper and torque the bolts back to spec (you can look up the torque spec for the make and model of your car online).
SAFETY TIP - GO SLOW AND LOOK FOR ANY FLUID LEAKING FROM THE BRAKE LINES --IF YOU NOTICE ANY LEAKING OR WETNESS AT ALL YOU WILL NEED TO REPLACE THE LINES THIS IS IMPERATIVE FOR SAFETY
Reattach and Tighten Wheel
Replace the wheel and tighten the lug nuts in a star pattern.

data.name: Diagnosing and Treating Copper Deficiency & Barber Pole Worms in Goats
data.about: A comprehensive guide for Nigerian Dwarf goat owners on identifying copper deficiency and parasitic infections, performing field tests, and administering treatments.
safety_notes: Never double-dose copper boluses; copper toxicity can be fatal.
Always ensure the goat's head is level during drenching to prevent aspiration pneumonia.
Consult a veterinarian if the goat's condition does not improve within 48 hours.

paragraphs.text: Diagnosing a Copper Deficiency in goats

A couple weeks ago, I came out to feed our two goats breakfast and my heart dropped --for the first time in the eight years he's been alive-- Totes (one of our wethered nigerian dwarf goats) did not want breakfast. I immediately started looking him over to see what could be wrong (I obviously assumed it was terminal cancer and I'd have to re-home McGoats so he didn't die of loneliness and depression). However, Other than not eating he was being pretty normal (still headbutting his brother McGoats away from his pile of oats (even though he didn't want to eat them) and still actively trotting around the barnyard, scratching himself against the fence. Besides his lack of appetite the only other things I noticed were: he seemed to be losing some of the hair on his tail, he was a bit bloated and he had loose stool instead of his normal bb pellets. I asked Gemini (Google's AI) about his symptoms and Gemini felt confident that he probably had a copper deficiency and possibly worms. I'd gotten lax about putting out goat minerals after the fifth or sixth time they knocked their mineral cups off of their hay manger, so I totally suck, but Gemini was pretty optimistic that I could remedy the situation.
Common symptoms of Copper Deficiency
hair loss, lethargy, and diarrhea.

When a goat has a healthy amount of copper in it's gut, the goat's immune system is better able to protect against worms and other parasites (which can become fatal), so unfortunately by getting lax with the mineral distribution I'd probably also exposed him to worms.
The FAMACHA Test: Diagnosing Barber Pole Worms in goats
Use the 'Cover, Push, Pull' method to check the inner lower eyelid.
Cover
Gently cover the goat's upper eyelid with your thumb.
Push
Gently push on the eyeball (this helps roll the lower eyelid out)
Pull
Pull the lower eyelid down to expose the inner mucous membrane.
Deep pink/red is healthy; pale pink or white indicates dangerous anemia most likely from Barber Pole worms.
Treating Goats For Worms
Gemini was pretty emphatic that I should NOT de-worm our goats unless I was sure they had worms.
apparently, livestock worms can easily become resistant to most dewormers if you deworm them too frequently or underdose when you do use dewormer.
Estimating Weight for Accurate Dosing

If you do not have a scale to weigh your goat, you can estimate a goats weight use the formula: ((Girth x Girth x Length) / 300) to find the approximate weight in pounds. Accurate weight is vital to avoid under-dosing, which can lead to dewormer resistance.
Administering the Dewormer

Draw the Safe-Guard dose (typically 1mL per 10lbs for goats). Let the goat bite and lick the syringe so it can get comfortable with it when the goat is still (restrained if necessary), slide the syringe into the side of the mouth behind the 'bars' of the teeth. **Slowly** depress the plunger toward the back of the tongue, let the goat swallow naturally.--DO NOT PLUNGE DOWN TOO FAST OR THE GOAT MAY CHOKE--
Administering Copper Boluses to Treat Copper Deficiency

According to Gemini, once a goat has started losing hair and/or become lethargic, its almost certainly too late to correct the situation with a normal, granular goat mineral mix. Instead, I should administer a copper boluse (a pill capsule full of tiny copper shavings) immediately and every six months thereafter --as well as making sure they have regular access to a goat mineral mix (like Manna Pro or Purina Goat Mineral which are the the brands I've used)

To administer the copper capsule, Gemini suggested I either put the bolouse in peanut butter or hide the pill inside a marshmallow, giving each goat an empty marshmallow followed by the marshmallow with the pill and then hold the third marshmallow up while they are just getting the second marshmallow (in order to get them excited about the upcoming treat so they would chomp less on the boloues). This was a total shit show when I tried it. Neither goat would accept a plain marshmallow, so I spread some peanut butter on them and as soon as I walked into the barnyard smelling like peanut butter they both started mauling me for the treats (and I couldn't even get footage). I was freaked out that one of them would eat two bolouses and overdoes on copper --which could be fatal-- so I kept my body in between them while I chucked the non-pill-pouch-marshmallows in opposite directions. Then I managed to get one bolouse-filled peanut butter marshmallow to each of the goats. It sort of seemed like they both gave the marshmallows a good few choms before they swallowed, but we're three weeks out and they seem to be back to being healthy rascally goats!
Monitoring and Recovery

After about 3-4 days, Totes poop consistency went back to being 'firm berries' and his appetite was returning to normal. About 8-10 days after the initial treatment, I Re-checked totes eyelid color to ensure the anemia was reversing. They were a nice deep pink already! Also that day, about 30-60 minutes after feeding him, I put my ear to his left flank to listen for 'gurgles' that indicated his digestion was active and normal (and it was). Now, after about three weeks, it even seems like Totes tail hair is starting to grow back.
If symptoms persist after 8-10 days

Accoring to Gemini, if diarrhea persists or eyelids remain white after 8 days, the goat may have Coccidiosis (which requires Sulfa drugs like Corid) or dewormer-resistant worms. Administer Fortified Vitamin B-Complex and Iron (Red Cell) to support red blood cell production. If 'Bottle Jaw' (swelling under the chin) appears or their temperature drops below 101.5°F, contact a vet immediately.

data.name: When Life’s Got You Stumped… Just Keep Digging
data.about: Turning unsightly stumps into head-turning landscape features
safety_notes: Use a GFCI-protected outlet when using corded tools near water.
Take breaks and be very careful not to injury your back when digging or lifting heavy stumps.
materials: succulents, seeds and/or young plants for planter

paragraphs.text: Digging Deeper

In order to make use of some of the luscious, productive dirt in the backyard of Arthur’s rental house, I decided to dig up an old tree stump and build a water garden. This was the 'brute force' approach: After a dozen or so 1-2 hour digging sessions, I finally got that gratifying 'timber' feeling of tipping the stump over. Once removed, the cavity became the perfect base for a lil' backyard pond. (See my water garden article for more details about planning and building a DIY backyard pond)
Burying My Problems

After two massive 'Lead' trees (Leucaena leucocephala) fell on my rental houses in Tempe, AZ, I removed the fall-prone species from my property and found myself swimming in stumps. Instead of digging my way out of the problem, I decided to build a raised garden bed around the largest cluster of stumps and bury them. However, Leucaena leucocephala are survivors and I've witnessed them quickly re-grow from stumps. After consulting with Gemini (Google's AI) I decided to use a 1/2-inch auger bit, to drill 10-inch deep holes into the stumps cambium layer and immediately filled the holes with Ferti-lome brush killer, hoping to reach the root system.

NOTE - The stump killer should be poured into the hole as soon as possible, so for maximum efficacy immediately pour stump killer in to each hole after its drilled (instead of waiting to pour it in several holes at once).
Sealing the Fate of Invasive Trees

After leaving the stumps uncovered for several days, I used a continuous roll of contractor trash bags to create a light-proof seal over the Tempe cluster. (Gemini recommended using a black tarp that's 4-6 mil or thicker --using the roll of contractor bags worked perfectly. Leaving the bags uncut provided a double-layer barrier that prevented 'suckers' from finding a path to the surface.)
Letting the Cycle of Life Continue

To finish the project, I built a circular wall around the stump cluster using Yukon Concrete blocks from home depot and an old irrigation berm as a natural edge. This allowed me to bury the treated stumps under a thick layer of mulch, compost, and dirt which helps maintain the moisture needed for fungi and bacteria to break down the wood while also creating a productive environment for shallow-rooting plants like strawberries and succulents.

data.name: DIY Kobmbucha - Brewing, Bottling, Harvesting and Restarting Kobmbucha
data.about: A comprehensive guide to 'flip'—harvesting kombucha, flavoring it for carbonation, and immediately starting your next batch using the same vessels.
safety_notes: Always ensure your hands and tools are rinsed with vinegar to avoid introducing unwanted bacteria.
Do not put your SCOBY in the fridge; keep it at room temperature to maintain its health.
Ensure the new tea is below 80°F before adding the SCOBY to prevent heat-kill.
tools: breathable, but tight woven cloth or paper e.g. t-shirt, pillow case, coffee filters, or paper towels (to cover jars)

paragraphs.text: Sourcing Supplies

A SCOBY (Symbiotic Culture of Bacteria and Yeast) is a slippery puck of life that you need to brew Kombucha. I've heard (from Google Gemini AI) that you can grow your own SCOBY using a bottle of store-bought kombucha or you may be able to find someone giving away or selling SCOBY from an online community. I was very excited to start this project though, so I bought a SCOBY online (for $15.00) from www.thekombuchashop.com . That site also sells jars for brewing and other accessories, but it was cheaper for me to buy two 80-oz jars of pickles from walmart and cut my SCOBY in half to brew two batches.
Note- To sterilize the jars and remove the pickle smell, (after I moved the pickles to smaller jars) I washed the pickle jars in my dishwasher.
Starting the Tea Base

The day my SCOBY was scheduled to arrive in the mail, I boiled 40 oz of water and steeped 12 tea bags (I used 6 green tea and 6 black tea bags) for 10 minutes. After removing the tea bags I stirred in 1.25 cups of granulated white sugar until dissolved and then divided the sweetened tea evenly between my two 80-oz jars and added the remaining cool filtered water to fill the jars almost to the top then set the jars aside to cool.
Livening it Up

When my SCOBY arrived, I doused my hands and a kitchen scissors with vinegar and cut open the pouch the SCOBY was shipped in. I poured about half of the 'starter liquid' (that the SCOBY was submerged in during shipping) into each jar, and then (did my best to) cut the SCOBY in half horizonally, placing one half of the SCOBY puck into each of my jars of room-temperature diluted sweet tea. This is your 'starter liquid' for the next batch.
Fermenting the deal

To protect the brewing Kombucha from contaminants from bugs and debris contaminating the batch (while still allowing it to breathe) I grabbed a couple of --freshly washed-- t-shirts out of the drier and used rubber bands to secure them over the opening at the top of the brewing jars. (If you don't want to use tshirts you can use another breathable, but tight woven cloth or paper like a pillow case, coffee filters, or paper towels etc). It's recommended to brew the jars at a temperature of 75F-85F for 7-14 days in a dark place, so I set the jars in a cabinet under our kitchen counter and waited for the magic to happen.
Checking In

I left the brewing Kombucha alone for the first week (not wishing to introduce contaminants) and then checked in on it on day seven. When I removed the t-shirts that were capping the jars, I saw that a new SCOBY puck was forming in each of the jars, but the new SCOBY were less than a quarter of an inch thick and looked odd to me. I showed a picture to Gemini (AI) and was told that my batch did not seem to be moldy or contaminated, so, I poked a clean straw under the SCOBY and had a little sip. It tasted sweet and a bit earthy, but it didn't have the vinegar tang I was used to from store-bought Kombucha. Our kitchen hasn't been above 72F lately, so I moved the jars to an upper cabinet and checked back after another week. It was starting to get a bit of faint vinegaryness, but still didn't have the tartness I wanted, so I gave it another 3 days, re-tasted and BOOM there was that familiar Kombocha tartness.
NOTE- If there's no tartness after 18-20 days, you may need to scrap it and start over.
Out with The Old in With the New

I poured 2-3 cups of the brewed kombucha into a clean bowl to use as starter liquid for the next batch. Then, with vinegar-cleaned hands, I remove the SCOBYs from the brew jars and placed them into the starter liquid. (This protects the SCOBY and keeps the bacteria active while you bottle the rest.)
Flavoring and Bottling (F2)

I'd been saving the bottles from the store-bought Kombucha I've been drinking lately, so I sterilized ten bottles and lids to use for my homebrew kombucha --Gemini (AI) recomends using pop-top bottles. I added 1 tsp minced ginger, 1 tsp lemon juice, 1/2 tsp lemon zest, and 1/2 tsp of sugar to each bottle. Using a funnel, I poured with the remaining kombucha into the jars, leaving 1 inch of headspace before tightly sealing the jars and storing them in my brewing cupboard for 4 days (for the second fermentation).
NOTE- I read that making ginger lemonade is an easy beginner recipe for flavored Kombucha, but there are lots of recipes online for other fun interesting kombucha brews.
The Immediate Restart

Once the ginger lemonade Kombucha was off to the cabinet, I made a new batch of diluted green and black sweet tea, poured the cooled sweet tea mixture into my original jars, divide the saved SCOBYs and starter liquid back into the brew jars, re-covered them with fresh clean t-shirts (secured with rubber bands) and my next batch has officially begun!
NOTE - The finished Kombucha should be good in the fridge for at least a month. Also when you drink it, you might want to strain it into a glass to avoid an overload of ginger pulp and lemon zest.

data.name: Frankensteining Dog Toys

paragraphs.text: Step 1: Prep the Toys

Select a variety of old dog toys that are still structurally sound. Using a screwdriver or a similar tool, carefully poke holes through the center or sides of each toy where you want the rope to pass through.
Step 2: String the Centipede

data.name: Making a Garden for our Chickens (that gets watered with pond runoff)
data.about: An Alluvial Plain For Our Hens
safety_notes: Wear Gloves and Be Careful Not To Snag Your Clothes on the Hardware Cloth while Cutting it.
tools: Tin Snips, Drill with Screw Bit, (electric) Miter Saw
materials: Hardware Cloth (or similar galvanized wire mesh)
Washers (to thread over the screws and hold down the Hardware Cloth

paragraphs.text: Learning from Papa YouTube

When I was getting ready to get back to having a backyard chicken flock (a few years ago), I thought it would be cool to plant a garden in the outdoor part of my chicken coop full of plants chickens love to eat. They went absolutely crazy for the garden the first day I let them into their coop. Actually, they loved it to death... Within the first week of moving into their coop they reduced it to dust.

It seemed obvious at that point that chickens and gardens just can't co-exist. And then papa YouTube came through with a DIY fix for me to try! A short hit my youtube feed that showed a guy using hardware cloth screwed to 2x4s to make a frame that protected the roots and base of a patch of grass from his chicken's talons, while still allowing them to graze.
Brass Tacks
Using a tape measure and miter saw, I cut some scrap 2x4s and 2x6s to make a wooden frame.

Then I measured a length of Hardware Cloth to fit over the frame. After I gloved up and cut the Hardware Cloth (with tin snips), I used washers threaded onto deck screws to secure the hardware cloth to the frame boards which loosely secured the frame together. I didn't feel like I needed my frame to be super secure since its meant to lie flat on the ground.
An Alluvial Plain for Chickens

The spot I selected for my chickens garden is enclosed within the fencing of their outdoor coop area and right next to the little pond I made in my barnyard. (Originally I was going to have the pond hook around and flow partially into the outdoor coop, but I mis-measured and it ended up that my pond liner could not go that far). That miscalculation created a little alluvial plain situation in the coop though.

After adding some compost and leveling the soil on the chickens' flood plain, I sprinkled some seeds, covered them with more compost and set the Hardware Cloth on top. The next day when I topped off the barnyard pond, some overflow water flowed into the chicken garden area and watered the seeds.
Much to the delight of my flock, within a couple weeks grass, sunflowers, peas, wheat and lettuce were starting to poke through the Hardware Cloth
It's early days so I don't know how often I'll have to re-seed or if the plants will survive the summer heat, but so far our hens are enjoying their salad bar!

data.name: Bracing For Summer: Building a Cool Dugout for our Desert Chickens
data.about: How I turned a muddy goat platform into a permanent, structured cooling station for my chickens to escape the summer heat.
safety_notes: Ensure the wooden platform is fully supported by cement blocks before allowing animals near it.
Check for any sharp edges on the blocks or platform that could injure the birds.

paragraphs.text: Phase 1: Observation

Our chickens subliminally commissioned me to build them a dugout in our barnyard. I noticed they were constantly hanging around our goats' wooden platform, scratching up the cool mud (wet from me dragging the hose around to fill water buckets) and lying in the shade by the base. As summer approaches, I always try to look for natural ways to help our flock keep cool, so I decided to lean into the vibe the chickens were cultivating and make the space more accessible and permanent.
Phase 2: Excavation and Reinforcement

Using a shovel and a garden hoe, I dug out the area under the wooden box to create a deep enough hollow for several chickens to fit comfortably. To prevent the platform from sagging and stop dirt from filling the new hole, I placed cement blocks at the corners to provide a solid, structural foundation.
Wallowing in Success

I filled the hole with water to get some evaporative cooling going and as soon as the water had seeped into the ground, the chickens immediately moved in. I think this new dugout will be a great addition to our summer cooling strategy. It stays significantly cooler than the surrounding ground, and the overhead cover provides shade and a sense of security for our flock. It’s a simple, low-cost way to keep the flock comfortable during the peak of summer without relying on electricity or ice.

data.name: Building a Predator Defense for a Mixed Barnyard
data.about: How to mount a motion-activated sprinkler to a permanent structure and use a dedicated timer for precision predator defense that won't terrorize your livestock.
safety_notes: Ensure all electrical connections on timers are weather-protected.
Test the 'arc' of the sprinkler manually to ensure it clears all structures.
materials: t-post or other post (to mount sprinkler)
Old rubber bike grip or inner tube (Shim)

paragraphs.text: A Mildly Offensive Defense

After a recent cat-attack in our chicken coop, I wanted to create a defense system that would reliably deter predators (if I forgot to close the chicken coop etc) while not getting destroyed by our goats. My go to AI recommended a perimeter defense sprinkler - basically a powerful sprinkler controlled by a light sensor. I liked the idea, but I could tell the recommended setup would not work with our scratch-happy goats around. The solution for us was to use an existing post from an RV cover to mount the sprinkler. However, a livestock fence post (t post) would probably have worked as well.
Securing the Security System

To keep the sprinkler from sliding down the smooth metal RV pole, I wedged a rubber bike grip beside the scrap wood --that I was using as a spacer to allow the sprinkler head enough clearance to rotate without hitting the pole.

To secure the sprinkler setup to our RV pole, I connected two sets of two hose clamps together (at the top and bottom of the scrap wood piece) creating loops large enough to envelop our square pole and the sprinkler, tightening them down with a screwdriver. Note - a second pair of hands would have been nice for this part of the job, but I was able to get by alone.
Dialing it In

The built in day/night mode was not working reliably for the sprinkler I bought, so I Install a digital hose timer at the faucet that was feeding the sprinkler and set the sprinkler sensor to 'Always On' (letting the timer dictate the exact minutes the system receives water). To fool-proof the system from letting this fool (me) forget to swap out the batteries, I set up a delivery subscription to receive some fresh AAs (to power the sprinkler sensor) every three months.

data.name: Limping a haggard watersack along for a second summer
data.about: Limping a haggard watersack along through one more season.
safety_notes: Ensure all electrical connections are weather-protected.
materials: Replacement Pool Parts as needed (motor, hoses etc)

paragraphs.text: Assessing the Damage

A water sack, or ✌️above ground pool✌️ as some folks call it, is basically a giant vinyl bag with an inflatable ring or metal frame to hold it up. Between the dogs, the gravel, thorny plants and chlorine, they don't last long for us. 2-3 years (at the most) and getting a full second or third season takes work. This year, in addition to the normal dog-claw punctures on the side walls and gravel poke through leaks on the bottom of the pool, a rat chewed off an important part of our pump casing, so we had to find a suitable replacement.
Prepping The Pool Area

Bottom-of-the-pool leaks are rarely a big deal. The calcification from our hard water and the pool chemicals, along with the layer of cardboard I put down under the pool and the weight of the water bearing down on the bottom holes, helps to naturally stop those leaks within a few days.
Patching Dry Leaks

If there are big holes that are noticeable before the pool is filled --or in the inflatable ring of an inflatable ring pool--, we usually patch those with adhesive vinyl pool patches on both sides of the hole or by spreading shoe goo (or silicone caulk) on the hole with painters tape on the outside.
Patching Wet Leaks

If a hole springs up after the pool is filled, you can try a vinyl patch, but if you can't get the area dry enough to make it stick, squeeze a glob of silicone caulk or shoe goo onto the outside of the hole and quickly tape over it with painters tape.
Replacing The Motor

For our 16 ft diameter x 48 inch pool, the recommended motor capacity is 1000 Gallons Per Hour. It wasn't hard to find an affordable replacement pump on Amazon (about $60.00), but unfortunately the hoses that came with the pump were slightly smaller than the hoses that originally came with the pool. So the night after we filled the pool, the hoses (and the plastic hose clamps that came with them), popped off the pool and let half the water out.
Replacing the plastic hose clamps with metal (automotive) hose clamps seems to have resolved that issue though.

data.name: Co-Authoring with Code: Using an LLM as a writing partner without losing your voice
data.about: A peek behind the curtain at how I use AI to smash writer's block, ensure my sci-fi is sci-believable, and keep my voice clear while drafting a book.
safety_notes: Remember to periodically roll your shoulders back and tuck your chin to prevent that 'computer hunch'.
materials: Caffeine, snacks and whatever else you need to stay fueled and keep yourself behind your keyboard.

paragraphs.text: Stocking Your Toolbox and Finding your Muse - Setting up a Narrative Framework

Writing processes are personal. Some authors like to put their fingers to the keyboard and just see where they wander --let the 'muse' work through them. I can't pull that off. The blinking cursor on the blank page is too daunting for me. Then there's the modern, 'I'm an idea person' folks who just give an AI a kernel of an concept and let it do everything. To me that's only fun if you are looking for a quick bedtime story. Unlike my construction projects, when it comes to writing, I like to really plan things out before I start. I want to know where something is going before I bother to really start down the path of writing prose, so I start with a conecept and then I assemble a 'box of tools' to help transform my idea into (what I hope is) art.

The tools I'm using for my current project (a sequel to my LitRPG novella, Hyperspear) are: my own brain, Google Docs (my writing space) and Google Gemini LLM (My AI writing partner, editor and technical advisor). Besides the fact that its free, the thing that I love most about Google Docs is the Document Tabs feature. This feature creates a side nav bar with quick links to isolated sub-documents within my project. For example, I have several document tabs for background information like settings and character bios (so I can keep my characters' personalities, narrative voice and physical appearances consistent etc). I also have a document tab for each chapter I intend to include in my finished work.

I only have four chapters entirely drafted at this point, but in my 'story arc tab' I broke my narrative arc into 12 chapters, so I also have document tabs for the chapters I haven't started started drafting. Having the future chapter tabs is really nice because it gives me a way to compartmentalize plot ideas, bits of dialogue and philosophy that I want to include -- as the ideas come to me. Then when its time for me to work on the chapter, instead of starting from scratch (and having to stare down a blank page), I just have to connect my ideas and flesh them out. So maybe the muse does speak to me, just on her own schedule.

Gemini has an option to allow users to create a 'notebook' where you load documents from drive, websites, local files or just paste text and the LLM will continue to reference back to those documents whenever you pose a query in that 'notebook'. However, that process doesn't work well for me --because (at least at this stage of my editing process), I'm constantly changing (and therefore invalidating) the content of the files I've uploaded.
A writing partner who can do it all - Using AI as a technical advisor and editor

To appease the 'those physics aren't realistic' trolls out there, I try to vet every scientific detail through AI --from the technical specs for an AI that can pilot an interstellar space ship to the celestial coordinates of the Alpha Centauri System Boundary.

LLMs are also really good at grammar. I've struggled my whole life to understand the right place to put a comma and an em dash, but TBH I don't want to waste brain space on perfecting punctuation, I'd rather offload that struggle onto an Gemini (when I'm doing final revisions) and stay focus on the creative work.
Sometimes, I also like to paste my work so far into a new Gemini workbook (or chat) and ask it to summarize what it thinks is going on in each chapter and identify any inconsistencies.
Keeping an Air Gap - Using an LLM without losing your voice

I keep an 'air gap' from AI by not using Gemini within the Google docs application and when I've got my plot stuck in a hole, need to check my science or want to check that something is coming across clearly, I cut and paste small sections of my prose into a Gemini chat and when it gives me suggestions for revisions, I copy and paste Gemini's revised text into my Google Doc above my original text and create a third chunk of text where I manually merge Gemini's ideas into my own, striking out the text I've used or decided to ditch until my original text and the revised text are completely struck through. Once I've the merged text, I delete my original text and gemini's text from the document, leaving only the merged section.

Once I'm happy with a draft of an entire chapter, I paste it into Gemini, ask it to check for grammar and consistency errors and let me know what it finds. Then I manually implement the corrections in Google docs. From my experience, even if Gemini is just supposed to be checking grammar, it can't help itself from changing or embellishing my prose when it edits them -- often in a way that detracts from the intended vibe of my work.
Print Hard Copies

Its nice to have things in the cloud, but cost-free storage is limited and every once in a while even Google has outages, so I always print each chapter as soon as I have a finished draft. Also, there's something nice about feeling the heft of the pages you wrote in your hands.

data.name: Propagating a Water Lily Using Reclaimed Pond Muck
data.about: Give a water lily rhizome a head start in nutrient-rich pond muck before transplanting it into a new pond.
safety_notes: Wash your hands thoroughly after handling wild pond muck and organic debris.
Be careful on slippery rocks when lifting heavy, water-logged planting bags out of/ into the pond.
tools: Paper coffee filter or piece of burlap
materials: Pea gravel or small river rocks

paragraphs.text: Harvesting the Reclaimed Soil

We end up with a lot of barnyard debris in our little pond. Over the years its started to build up into a nice soil that our water lily loves. Earlier this year, I had tried to plant a water lily in the pond I made at friend's house, but it died shortly after sporuting leaves. For my second attempt, I'm using some of our home grown nutrient-rich pond sludge (instead of soil from amazon) and I'm letting the plant grow in an existing pond before transplanting to the new water garden. PRO TIP - The pond muck is highly fertile, so it acts as a perfect natural fertilizer for the new water lily.
Bagging and Planting

To prevent the fine muck from escaping and clouding the water, line the inside of a mesh pond plant bag with a paper coffee filter or a piece of burlap. Using a trowel or gloves transfer the built up soil from the bottom of the pond to the planter bag. Plant the store-bought rhizome at a 45-degree angle, ensuring the growing tips or 'eyes' point upward and remain slightly exposed above the soil line. Top the soil with a layer of pea gravel to hold everything in place.
(optional) Harvesting a Rhizome Division

If you have a healthy plant that's been growing for several years, and you don't want to buy a new plant, you can easily harvest a clone from an established lily. Reach into the pond and locate the thick, horizontal root system. Find a natural joint where a side branch or 'pup' with visible growth buds has formed and cut the bud away from the main root system. Or, if you don't want to use a knife you can gently bend the joint until it snaps cleanly off—much like breaking a piece of fresh ginger. Ensure your harvested section is 3 to 5 inches long with at least one healthy bud before planting it into the prepared muck bag.
The Shallow Nursery Period

Create a 'nursery' for the new plant, by placing the bag in a shallow depth. This allows the warm sun to stimulate rapid growth. Submerge the planting bag on a pond shelf where there are about 3 to 6 inches of water over the top of the bag. Within 4 to 7 days, you should see tiny leaf spikes emerge and start growing toward the surface.
Transferring to the New Pond

Once the plant has established a strong root system and has 4 to 5 mature lily pads floating flat on the surface (typically 4 to 5 weeks), it is ready to move.  To protect it from hungry snails and sudden depth changes, prop the bag up on bricks so the existing leaves comfortably reach the surface, gradually lowering it as the stems grow longer.

data.name: BUDGET-FRIENDLY RENTAL PROPERTY WIRE FENCE INSTALLATION
data.about: When the best defence is a fence.
safety_notes: Always call 811 or your local utility line locator before driving any posts into the ground.
Wear heavy-duty leather work gloves to protect your hands from sharp wire ends and heavy steel tools.
Keep your feet clear and wear sturdy boots when operating a heavy manual T-post driver.
tools: Tin snips or Wire cutters / Linesman pliers
Sawzall and/or hedge trimmers (if there are small stumps or branches to be removed)
materials: Gate post(s) hinges and pipe clamps
Quickrete or similar fast setting concrete for gate posts
(optional) Hardware to attach fencing to existing masonary

paragraphs.text: So apparently all of my tenants have caught the next door neighbor being some kind of package steeling porch pirate, so I decided the best defence is . . . a fence.
CLEARING AND PREPPING THE FENCE LINE

To prep the fenceline, we cleared away loose dirt, gravel, weeds, and debris along the intended boundary using a rake and shovel. In our case, there were also some small stumps and branches protruding from bushes, so we used a Sawzall and hedger trimmers to clear those out of the way. Clearing a path ensures that fencing sits flat against the grade and prevents shifting soil from burying the bottom edge of the wire over time.
DRIVING THE T-POSTS

Before driving the posts in we laid them on the ground, spacing them about 6 to 8 feet apart. It's good to visualize the spacing before diving in so you can adjust for obstacles in the ground etc(we had previously had a lot of buried concrete to work around from an old chain-link fence that the city made me take down during construction of my additional dwelling unit). To use the Fence Post Driver, slide it over the top of each post, lift the driver and drop it firmly to pound the post into the ground until the anchor plate is completely submerged and secure (This is an excellent glute and core work out). NON-PRO TIP - If you don't have a fence post driving tool, you can just use a heavy sledgehammer to pound the posts in (This is Arthur's preferred method).
UNROLLING AND SECURING THE WIRE FENCING

It was helpful to have two of us get started on securing the actual galvanized, welded wire fencing to the posts: I held the end while Arthur unfurled the roll along the outside of the driven T-posts and secured the wire ties to the first post. After that he was able to continue unrolling and securing it on his own while I worked on prepping the next section of the fence line. PRO TIP - secure the mesh to the ridges on the T-posts in at least 3 places, ensuring the fence is taut from top to bottom to prevent sagging.
INSTALLING THE GATE

To finish the enclosure and add a gate, we set a chainlink corner post two feed in the ground using a 50 lb bag fo Quickcrete. (The set time varies depending on the concrete you're using and the temp/humidity). PRO TIP: Use a level when setting the post to ensure it's perfectly upright before you leave it to set in the concrete. After the concrete was set, to secure the gage to the post, we fastened heavy-duty pipe clamps and gate hinges using an adjustable (channel lock) wrench and a drill with ratchet attachments. PRO TIP: Adjust the placement of the hinges on the post/ gate to ensure the gate is properly aligned, clearing the ground completely and swinging smoothly.

data.name: ADDING SUPPORT TO A WOODEN RAISED GARDEN BED USING HARDWARE CLOTH
data.about: A Metal Diaper to Stop Soil Leaks. . . hopefully.
safety_notes: Wear Gloves! The cut edges of hardware cloth are sharp!
tools: Tin snips or Wire cutters / Linesman pliers

paragraphs.text: ALL WOOD THINGS MUST COME TO AN END

I built the raised garden bed that houses our herbs five or six years ago, and it's been holding up like a champion, but I noticed recently, that some of the planks underneath have been falling and starting to expose soil, so I decided to wrap some hardware cloth around the bottom to add support.
ANCHORING THE HARDWARE CLOTH

I had some scrap wood on hand and I'm not too concerned about the aesthetics, so I used scrap wood instead of washers to pin the hardware cloth to the outside frame. PRO TIP - when pinning boards to the side or bottom of things it's usually easier if you start the screws in the wood on the ground.
WIRING UP THE ENDS

One end of the 'cloth' was sagging (after I secured it to the ends), so I wound some 20 gauge wire --clockwise-- around a couple of screws that I started in the frame and *slowly* drove those screws in until they were taught and the 'cloth' was no longer drooping.
CUTTING AROUND LEGS

To wrap the entire underside of the garden bed in my metal diaper, I had to go around a central support leg. I called in Arthur for support on this part. It was helpful to have him pull the fabric taught while I cut the fabric around the leg.
SWADDLED LIKE A NEWBORN
Overall it was a pretty quick and easy process that *hopefully* will extend my garden's life for years to come!

data.name: DIY QUICK-REVEAL POSTER SCROLL
data.about: How to build a lightweight, portable, quick-reveal hanging poster scroll using simple materials—perfect for solo stage performers needing a hands-free prop setup.
safety_notes: Take care when using scissors or utility knives to cut your dowels and tape.
Ensure your hanging string is securely tied so the scroll does not slip off the mic stand mid-performance.
materials: Printed Poster (approx. 24 x 36 inches or preferred size)
Two Wooden Dowels (slightly wider than your poster)
20 gauge wire (to make a flexible hook for hanging on mic stands etc)

paragraphs.text: PREPPING FOR A PROP COMEDY ADVENTURE

Arthur, his brother and I are doing dry July right now, so we've been looking for new ways to fill our evenings. A couple weeks ago, we went to an open mic at a comedy club. Everyone was friendly and it seemed way less intimidating than what I'd expected, so I wrote a set and came back the next week and went up. I got some laughs and I guess it went to my head because I immediately came home and decided I wanted to go back again and try my hand a prop comedy... so anyway, here is my design for the poster scroll prop I'm planning to use.
BRING IN THE REINFORCEMENTS

Since I assume I will have a long comedy career and use this prop over and over for many years, I decided it's important to protect the edges of the paper from tearing under the weight of the dowels, so I applied blue painter's tape along the entirety of the top and bottom edges. PRO TIP: Fold the tape evenly over both sides of the paper to create a secure, reinforced border.
ATTACHING THE DOWELS AND HANGING STRING

I also used painters tape to attach the dowels. I put one wooden dowel at the very top edge and the second dowel at the very bottom edge of the poster then used additional strips of painter's tape to secure the dowels firmly to the reinforced edges. I had a scrap of heavy smooth metal on hand from another project, so I taped that to the bottom dowel (with painters tape). Then I cut some bailing twine and tied it securely to both outer ends of the top dowel to create a hanger.
THE HOOK

The top string that's affixed to the dowel is probably enough to hold the poster in place on the mic stand, but to make sure it stays, I made a small hook out of 20 gauge wire ---that I wrapped with painters tape to prevent scratching the pic or mic stand. I attached the hook to the center of the string on the top dowel and now I can thread it through the mic stand or twist it around the base if necessary
DRAMATIC REVEAL

To roll up the scroll for transport, I laid the poster image-side up and rolled from the bottom dowel upward (keeping the image inward to protect the print). Then I secured the rolled scroll with loose rubber bands. When it's time to use the poster, I plan to hook the wire hook through or over the mic stand, remove the rubber band, and let the weighted bottom dowel fall to dramatically unfurl the poster.
ONE LAST TRICK UP MY SLEEVE

To add an extra sprinkle of humor on top of my set, I'm also planning to stash a telescoping bunny ear antena (that I unscrewed from our TV receiver) up my sleeve or from an inside pocket and then pull it out and extend it to use as a pointer during my poster presentation (where I go through my dating history showing that I've dated some version of everyone from the 90s Burger King Kids club). The final cherry on top of my prop comedy set is a picture of Arthur that I velcro onto the poster to give a visual comparison of how my current boyfriend is a combination of Kid Vid and the calculator in his pocket nerd.
